events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Omar proposes Omar, Kenji. Omar leads mission 1 and proposes a team of Omar and Kenji. Both are trustworthy from my perspective, and including myself keeps the team fully under good control while I avoid signaling any private knowledge.

I'm comfortable being on the team, but I have no evidence about Omar's alignment. This is a reasonable opening proposal from my perspective, though a successful mission alone wouldn't prove either player is good.

I'll be blunt about the process rather than about any player, because at this stage none of us has evidence about anyone. What we do have is a proposal where both slots went to the proposer and to a player who immediately said he has no information at all about the other person on the team. That is a team that can produce no signal for the rest of the game — two people who, by their own admission, are only vouching for themselves.

So my preference is to keep the leader on the team, since a leader who puts himself out there is at least being visible and accountable, and to swap the second slot for the one player nobody has spoken about yet: Leo. If Leo goes on mission 1, we at least learn something about him and about how a different pair behaves, and we avoid a team built entirely out of mutual self-trust. That is a better information position for the council than Omar and Kenji.

Kenji, I want to be fair to you: you haven't claimed anything false, and I don't think you're hiding anything. My point is only that your presence on this specific team adds no information for us, and it's the natural place to make the change while the cost is lowest.

Omar, you said including yourself keeps the team fully under good control. Do you have anything beyond that reasoning to justify why the second slot should be Kenji rather than Leo, and would you accept swapping Kenji for Leo if you do not?

Isha, to answer you directly: I'm keeping Kenji because he has been consistent and I have no reason to distrust him, and I won't swap him for Leo. Leo hasn't spoken at all, so swapping him in just to create information is a gamble, not a safeguard. You say this team produces no signal, but an untested player doesn't add signal either. You're pushing the swap hard and naming Leo without any evidence about him, so my question back to you: what specifically makes Leo the right choice over Kenji, beyond the fact that he hasn't been named yet?

Omar, directly answering your question: what makes Leo better than Kenji is not that I know anything about Leo — I know nothing about Leo — but that I know something about Kenji, and it is that Kenji's own words reduce his marginal value to zero on this specific proposal. Kenji told the council he has no evidence about anyone, including you. So the slot he occupies tells the council nothing it cannot already infer, while Leo is the only player in this game whose alignment we have zero read on.

On your point that an untested player is not a safeguard: I agree, and I am not claiming Leo is safe. I am claiming the council is blind, and blind councils make bad decisions on missions two through five as well. Right now we have exactly two data points on the table and both of them come from the same conversation. If Leo goes on mission 1 and the mission succeeds, we have a second pair, a second behavior pattern, a second set of results to reason about. If it fails, we learn that early instead of on mission four, when it is far more expensive. Either branch is information; Kenji's branch is not.

On cost: the cost of being wrong here is one vote and one discussion. The cost of a council that never tested anyone is that we carry our ignorance into the three missions that decide this game. I would also note the pattern I dislike in the proposal as it stands: the leader takes the first slot and pairs with a player who explicitly declines to vouch for anyone, which makes the team's confidence entirely self-referential. That is a weak foundation, not a safe one.

I am not asking you to trust Leo. I am asking you to let the council see him once, before we are committed. If you keep Kenji, I understand why, and I will not call it bad faith — but I will remember that the reasoning was 'we know nothing about Leo' rather than 'we know something about Kenji.'

Isha, I'll answer your point directly. Kenji's saying he has no evidence about anyone is neutral. It doesn't make him suspicious, and it doesn't make Leo a better pick. You've now said twice that the swap is about getting information, but you've given no reason Leo would be safer to put on a mission than Kenji. An untested player is an unknown risk, and we would be swapping a known quantity for one. I'm not ready to change the team for that. My question is this: if Mission 1 succeeds with Omar and Kenji, what specific information would still be missing that you need, and why couldn't we test Leo on a later mission when we'd know more?

Omar, your question is fair and I'll answer it plainly, because it is the whole dispute.

You ask what information would still be missing if Mission 1 succeeds with you and Kenji. The honest answer is: almost everything. A success tells the council that the two people on that team did not sabotage it — nothing more. It says nothing about Maya, nothing about Leo, nothing about Isha, and nothing about Kenji beyond what Kenji already told us, which is that he has no read on anyone. One success with a self-referential pair is nearly the same as no information at all. And you ask why we couldn't test Leo later. We could, but later is strictly more expensive and less informative. Missions grow — a three-person team is a bigger commitment than a two-person one, and putting an untested player into a three-person team tells us less, not more, because the other two members' behavior muddies the read on him. The cheapest, cleanest test of an unknown player is the smallest one, and that window is right now, in this proposal, at no additional cost to the leader at all.

Your framing also has the logic inverted. You say an untested player is an unknown risk and that I am swapping a known quantity for one. But Kenji is not a known quantity — he said himself he knows nothing about anyone, including you. Nobody in this game is a known quantity yet. The only real difference between your proposal and mine is that yours picks a player who has declared himself blind, while mine picks the one player whose alignment the council has no read on whatsoever. Blind is not safer. Blind is just untested.

One more practical point, since we are talking about cost: leadership rotates. If this council's standing practice becomes "only test a player when the leader happens to favor it," then no one ever gets tested, because every leader will prefer the teammate who has already agreed to be on the team. The mission-one proposal is the cheapest place for this council to buy information, and it is the only place where the leader's own slot and one extra slot are all that stand between us and total ignorance going into the three missions that decide this game.

I'm not asking you to trust Leo, and I'm not accusing you of bad faith — I think you genuinely prefer consistency over exploration. But your consistency is choosing the arrangement that teaches us the least, on the grounds that consistency is a virtue in itself. I'd rather take one risk we understand in full than carry three missions of pure guessing.

Omar, would you change the second slot to Leo, or is there some specific reason you have for Kenji that you haven't stated yet?

Isha, to answer directly: the only reason I'm keeping Kenji is that he has been consistent and I have no reason to distrust him. I have nothing beyond that to add. Your case for Leo has stayed the same across several messages: he hasn't spoken, so the council learns nothing from him yet. That is true of any untested player, and it doesn't make Leo the better choice. Kenji saying he has no read on anyone is an honest statement, not a red flag, and you treat it as worthless while making Leo the one answer. You keep pressing for the same swap and the reasons keep changing, which is why I'm not moving. Mission 1 with Omar and Kenji still lets the council watch Leo on a later team. I'd like to hear from Maya and Leo before we vote.

I’ve been listening, and I don’t think either side has shown that Omar and Kenji are more dangerous than Omar and Leo. Kenji saying he has no read on anyone is neutral, not suspicious. Isha is right that a mission-one success would be weak evidence, because Evil can choose Success, but that weakness applies to any two-person team, including Omar and Leo. The concrete difference is that Omar and Kenji have spoken and Leo has not; that is not a safety argument for Leo. I’m inclined to approve the current team so the council gets a mission result rather than spending a rejection on a swap with the same underlying uncertainty. If the mission fails, that fail card is real information. If it succeeds, I’ll treat it as limited information and not as a blanket clearance. I’m not accusing anyone here; I just think we should not confuse “untested” with “safer.”

Since my name has been brought up extensively, I want to weigh in directly. I appreciate Isha's focus on council information, but I agree with Omar and Maya that being untested does not inherently make me a safer or better choice for Mission 1. Omar as the leader put forward a team he is comfortable with, and pushing to force an untested player onto the very first mission without cause doesn't strike me as necessary.

At this stage, any two-player team carries uncertainty. If the council is satisfied with seeing Omar and Kenji go forward to establish a baseline, I have no objection to letting this team run and judging them by the outcome. I don't believe we need to spend rejections trying to manufacture an alternate test when we can simply watch the result of the leader's proposal.
Omar confirms Omar, Kenji. I'm keeping Omar and Kenji for Mission 1. The swap to Leo is an untested gamble, and this lineup gives the council a clean result to build on.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Maya proposes Maya, Omar, Kenji. I know I am loyal, and Omar and Kenji delivered a clean Mission 1 result. Keeping that successful core with me gives the council continuity and a clear team to test.

Maya, I'll be consistent with what I argued on Mission 1, and that consistency now points at your proposal rather than against it.

Your team is Maya, Omar, Kenji — the exact pair that already ran, plus you. Mission 1 succeeded with Omar and Kenji, so what did we learn from that success? Only that two players did not sabotage. It told us nothing about you, nothing about Leo, and nothing about me. Now you propose to take that same untested slot again and fill it with yourself. We are two missions in, and the council's read on Leo is still exactly zero. The mission-one window I warned about was a two-person team; this is a three-person team, which is a larger commitment and a noisier test, not a cheaper one. If Leo goes on Mission 2 with two people who have already proven their baseline behavior, we get a much cleaner read on him than we ever would on Mission 4, when three other players' results muddy the water.

Let me be clear about what I am and am not claiming. I am not claiming Omar or Kenji failed Mission 1 — I voted against that team, but the result was a success and I am not pretending otherwise. I am not claiming you are hiding anything; you chose continuity, which is a legitimate instinct. But continuity in the second slot means the same player learns nothing new, and the person we have never tested stays on the bench again for no stated reason other than that he hasn't spoken yet. "Untested" was never "safe" — I said that last time too, and Leo himself agreed with me, which makes the argument stranger now: the player you would be replacing has already told the council he sees no reason to be on this team, while the untested player asked only that we watch a result.

Here is my concrete ask, Maya: swap Kenji for Leo and run Maya, Omar, Leo. You keep yourself and Omar, you preserve the successful pairing that gave you your baseline, and you buy the council the one piece of information we do not have. The cost is one vote and one discussion, and the benefit is that we finally stop guessing about Leo before the missions that decide this game.

Maya, would you take Maya, Omar, Leo, or is there a specific reason Kenji must be on Mission 2 beyond continuity with Mission 1?

Isha, I’ll answer your ask directly. I’m not treating Mission 1 success as a clearance, and I agree it only tells us Omar and Kenji did not fail that mission. But that is still a concrete result, and your alternative replaces Kenji with Leo without adding any evidence that Leo is safer. You say the value is information, not safety; I accept that distinction. My question is about cost and timing: in this five-player game, Mission 3 is also a two-person mission, so the clean small test you want is available next mission, while Mission 2 is a three-person commitment. I would rather not reject a team that includes the only pair with a successful result in order to run the same experiment one mission earlier. My team keeps Omar and Kenji because they have at least produced a mission result together, and includes me because I know I am loyal. It does not clear Leo, and it does not clear me to anyone else. If this team fails, that is real information and I will treat it that way. If it succeeds, I will still not treat it as blanket clearance. Isha, if Mission 3 is a two-person team, what specific reason makes testing Leo on Mission 2 worth rejecting this team rather than waiting for that cleaner window?

Maya, direct answer first: the reason to test Leo now rather than on Mission 3 is that Mission 3's two-person window is not ours to spend. Leadership rotates, and by Mission 3 the proposal may come from someone whose instinct is exactly the continuity instinct you are using right now — two players with an established result, no untested slot. "We can test him later" assumes a later proposal we will also get to shape. We have this one, and it is the only one where the swap is costless to the leader's own position.

Second, the noisiness argument is backwards. You say a three-person team muddies the read on Leo. But Omar and Kenji are the same two people, with the same demonstrated behavior, so the two anchor slots produce the same signal they produced on Mission 1. Maya plus Omar plus Leo is a controlled test with two constant slots and one variable. Maya plus Omar plus Kenji is three slots, two of which we have already observed and one of which you have just told us you own — "I know I am loyal." That is not a variable, it is a constant you declared. So the marginal information from your team over Mission 1 is close to zero. Leo is the only slot on either proposal that produces a read the council does not already have.

Third, on cost. A rejection is one of five we are allowed, and it is not only a loss: it hands the proposal to a different leader who may include the player we want to see. Isha is not claiming that a rejection is free. Isha is claiming that the argument for waiting is a forecast about a future proposal, while the argument for acting now is about the one in front of us.

I want to be precise about what I am not saying. I am not saying you are hiding something, and I am not saying Omar or Kenji failed anything — they succeeded, and I voted for the team that ran. I am saying the council has now bought the same information twice and is about to buy it a third time, and that the one player with zero read stays on the bench because nobody has yet stated a reason that is about Leo rather than about habit.

Maya, will you take Maya, Omar, Leo — or is there something specific about Kenji that goes beyond continuity with Mission 1 and beyond the fact that he was already on the last successful team?

Isha, direct answer: I will not swap Kenji for Leo on this proposal. The specific reason is not merely habit; it is that Kenji has actually been on a mission and produced a result with Omar, while Leo has not. I agree that does not clear Kenji and that a success is weak evidence, but it is the only concrete mission behavior we have. Replacing Kenji with Leo now does not make the team safer; it changes one unknown for another while discarding the only completed pair. I also disagree that this is a costless test: a rejection spends one of our five and hands leadership to someone else, so “we can test Leo later” is not guaranteed by acting now. Mission 3 is a two-person mission, which is the cleaner small window Isha described, and I would support using that window for Leo if the proposal reaches a leader willing to do it. For this vote, I prefer continuity plus a real result: Maya, Omar, Kenji. I will not treat a success as blanket clearance for anyone.

I have made my case twice now and Maya has declined twice, so let me be careful to state what I actually want rather than repeat myself.

I want Leo on Mission 2. Not because I have evidence about Leo — I have none, and I have said so every time — but because the council's information position is not improving. Mission 1 gave us one data point about one pair. Maya's proposal takes that same pair and adds a leader who has declared herself a constant, so the marginal information from this proposal over Mission 1 is close to zero. Every mission we spend without a read on Leo is a mission where the only person we know nothing about stays unobserved, and we are three missions from deciding this game.

Maya, your reply that Mission 3 is a two-person mission and therefore the cleaner window answers a question that was never the real one. The clean window is only clean if some leader in this game actually chooses to spend it that way. Leadership rotates to people whose instinct may well be continuity — the leader who has a proven pair proposes the proven pair. "We can test Leo later" is a forecast about a proposal that does not exist yet, made by people who will each act on their own reasoning. The proposal in front of us is real, and it is the one where a swap costs the leader's own position nothing.

I also accept your point about the cost of a rejection: it spends one of our five and passes the decision to someone else. That is a real cost and I am not going to pretend it is not. But the record so far shows this council voting down a swap and then approving a proposal containing the same untested gap one mission later, so the cost has not bought us a better outcome, only a delay.

I am not accusing anyone of bad faith. Maya, I think you genuinely value a completed result over an untested variable, and that is a coherent preference, not a hidden one. My concern is only that this council keeps choosing the arrangement that teaches us least. Maya, Omar, Kenji — if any of you think Leo belongs on this mission, say so now.

Isha, I don’t see a reason to replace me with Leo on this proposal. From my perspective, keeping me on the team preserves a loyal player, and the successful first mission gives some limited evidence about Omar. Maya remains untested, but adding her already gives us a new team composition. A success would not clear anyone, and a failure would not identify the saboteur. I’m inclined to approve this team rather than swap a known loyal player for someone whose alignment I don’t know.

I want to be clear about where I stand, especially since Isha has repeatedly advocated for swapping me in. I appreciate the argument about generating fresh information, but as I said during Mission 1, I'm not going to lobby to force myself onto a team just to be tested.

At the same time, Maya, Kenji, and Omar should remember that a clean Mission 1 is not proof of alignment—evil players regularly support Mission 1 specifically to secure spots on Mission 2. Bringing both Omar and Kenji forward does carry that risk. However, Maya has made her rationale clear, and the three of you appear aligned on testing this group. If Maya believes this continuity is our best baseline, I am content to let the mission run and hold all three members accountable to the result.

I'm backing Maya, Omar, and Kenji. This team includes the only pair with a clean mission result, and Maya has been open about why she chose it. Isha has pushed hard against this team, and her reasons have shifted from message to message: first that Mission 1 was blind, then that Mission 3 would not be ours to use, and now that Leo should go on this mission even though Leo says he won't lobby for a spot. The council should weigh that pattern. Leo, you said evil players regularly support Mission 1 to secure spots on Mission 2, yet you voted to approve that same Mission 1 team. What specific behavior on this proposal makes you think it is evil-driven, and what would you need to see from Maya, Kenji, or me to trust it? I'm not accusing you, but I'd like a concrete answer before we vote.

Omar, to answer your questions directly: I voted to approve Mission 1 because rejecting the very first proposal without any game data simply burns a vote without adding clarity. Letting you and Kenji run gave the council our first baseline result. However, approving Mission 1 to gather data is entirely different from assuming that result clears both of you permanently. I am not accusing you or Kenji of being evil; I am pointing out the structural reality that an evil player on Mission 1 has every incentive to play a Success card specifically to secure a spot on Mission 2. When Maya brings both of you forward together, she is trusting that neither of you made that play. My question to you, Omar, is: from Maya's perspective, do you believe carrying over both members of that pair simultaneously is truly a safe play, or do you recognize that if either one of you were evil, Mission 2 is effectively conceded?

Leo, to answer directly: I can speak for myself, and I am loyal. Carrying both Kenji and me forward is not a blind bet, because Mission 1 succeeded with us on it, which is limited evidence and not a clearance. You are right that a success does not prove either of us is good, and I am not claiming it does. But rejecting this team means swapping a pair with a shared result for an untested player, and nothing in this discussion has given a concrete reason to do that. Maya has explained her choice openly. Isha has argued against this team at every stage, and her reasons have changed from one message to the next, first that Mission 1 was blind, then that Mission 3 would be lost, and now that Leo must go on this mission. The council should weigh that pattern when it votes. I support approving Maya, Omar, Kenji.

I'm backing Maya, Omar, and Kenji. Omar and Kenji already produced a Mission 1 success, and Maya's proposal keeps that pair while adding a player who openly stated her loyalty. Isha has argued for a swap at every stage, and the swap is always Leo, who has not spoken for or against anyone. Her reasons have changed from message to message: first Mission 1 was blind, then Mission 3 would be lost, and now Leo must go on this mission. Leo, you said evil players may play Success on Mission 1 to reach Mission 2. That risk applies to any pair we send, including Omar and Leo, so it does not argue for Leo specifically. I have no reason to suspect Maya or Kenji. I will approve this team, and I ask the council to judge the proposal by the mission results it produces rather than by who pressed hardest against it.

Maya, Omar's confidence rests on the assumption that neither he nor Kenji played a quiet Success on Mission 1, which is completely circular from the rest of the council's viewpoint. As the leader and the only player on this proposal who wasn't on that first mission, are you genuinely comfortable betting our momentum entirely on that single pair being clean, or do you see any merit in breaking them up to hedge our risk?

Leo, directly answering your question: I am not claiming Omar and Kenji are proven clean, and I am not treating Mission 1 as a clearance. You are right that if either Omar or Kenji were Evil and played a quiet Success on Mission 1, this proposal carries that risk. But breaking them up does not remove that structural risk; it only changes which unknown the council is accepting. A team of Maya, Omar, and Leo would still depend on Omar’s Mission 1 behavior being honest, and it would replace a player who has at least produced a mission result with a player whose alignment I have no read on. That is not a hedge; it is a different bet. My reason for keeping Omar and Kenji is not that I believe a single Success proves them good. It is that this council has exactly one concrete mission behavior to build from, and I would rather use Mission 2 to test a team that includes me while preserving that pair than discard the only completed result for an untested swap. I know I am loyal, so from my perspective the team is not “the same pair with no new information”; it is the successful pair plus one loyal Servant. I also heard your warning that an Evil player could play Success on Mission 1 to secure Mission 2. That is true, but it applies to any pair, and it does not give me a specific reason to think Omar or Kenji did so. If this mission fails, that failure is real information, and I will treat it that way. If it succeeds, I will still not call the team cleared. I am comfortable approving Maya, Omar, Kenji for that reason, and I am not breaking up the pair merely to appear cautious.

Maya confirms Maya, Omar, Kenji. I am keeping Maya, Omar, and Kenji. Omar and Kenji produced the only completed mission result, and no specific evidence has been presented to justify replacing either with Leo. I am not treating Mission 1 as a clearance, but continuity plus my known loyalty gives the council a clear result to judge.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Kenji proposes Kenji, Omar. I know I am loyal. Omar and I succeeded together on Mission 1, and the same core succeeded on Mission 2, though neither result proves Omar is loyal.

Kenji’s proposal is Kenji and Omar. I’m judging it against what we actually know, not against the fact that it repeats a successful pair. Mission 1 succeeded with Kenji and Omar; Mission 2 succeeded with Kenji, Omar, and me. I know I am loyal, so Mission 2 does not independently prove either Kenji or Omar is good: a success only tells us no one on that team played Fail. That is real but limited evidence. The proposed team has the strongest completed record in the game, and I have not heard a specific reason to believe either Kenji or Omar is evil. Isha and Leo remain untested, and I understand the argument for using Mission 3’s two-person window on one of them. But rejecting this proposal would spend a vote and pass leadership to Isha; it would not guarantee a cleaner test happens. If this team succeeds, I will not treat it as a blanket clearance, especially with the assassination still ahead. If it fails, that fail card is real information and should shape Mission 4. On balance I am inclined to approve Kenji and Omar, while holding the result to the same standard I applied to Missions 1 and 2. I am not accusing anyone.

Kenji, this proposal is the exact pattern I have been arguing against for two missions, and I want to say clearly that I am not changing my position — I am applying it to the team in front of us now.

The team is Kenji and Omar. That pair has now been together twice, and both times the mission succeeded. So the only concrete mission behavior this council owns concerns these two players, and it has already been collected. Meanwhile the council's read on Leo is still exactly zero, two missions after I first asked for him to be tested. Mission 3 is a two-person mission, which means this is the smallest and cleanest team this game can produce, and it is the last time a leader can spend a slot on a player nobody has observed without muddying the test against other teammates. A three-player team on Mission 4 would tell us far less about Leo than a two-player team here does, because the second slot would be a variable instead of a constant.

I also want to name the dynamic plainly, without accusing anyone of bad faith. Each of the last three proposals has been built by taking the pair with the established result and adding the leader. Kenji is doing exactly that here. If that pattern continues, no player who has not yet been sent on a mission will ever be sent, because the argument for a swap is always a forecast about a future proposal that some future leader will make, and the argument against is always about a result we already hold. Isha understands that a rejection costs one of our five, and Isha is not claiming a rejection is free — but the cost of a rejection is one vote, and the cost of never testing the one player the council knows nothing about is that we carry our ignorance into the two missions and the assassination that decide this game.

So my concrete ask, Kenji: propose Leo in the second slot instead of Omar, or Omar instead of Kenji — either swap gives the council a read on the only player it has never observed, and neither of them has given a reason specific to Kenji or Omar that goes beyond continuity with the previous results. Leo himself has said he will not lobby for a spot, and he should not have to; this is about what the council knows, not about Leo's campaigning.

Kenji, is there something specific to Omar, beyond the fact that the two of you have already run together twice, that makes him the right second member over Leo — and if not, will you take Leo for the second slot?

Isha, I have no specific evidence that Omar is loyal beyond our two successful missions together. Those results do not clear him, but I know I am loyal, and he has twice chosen Success alongside me. I have no comparable mission evidence about Leo, so I prefer to keep Omar rather than make that swap.

Testing Leo might give us information, but information is not the only goal: a successful Mission 3 takes us straight to assassination, so there may be no later mission on which to use it. I’m keeping Kenji and Omar, while recognizing that an Evil Omar could have supported the earlier missions.

I have pressed hard for Leo across two discussions, so I want to state clearly where I stand now rather than repeat myself a third time.

My objection to this team has always been informational: the council owns exactly one piece of mission behavior — a pair that has now run twice — and has never observed Leo at all. That objection is still true. But I need to correct something I implied earlier: I treated the existence of a later, smaller testing window as a fact, when in truth it is a forecast about a proposal that does not exist yet, made by leaders who will each act on their own reasoning. Kenji's point is correct that a Mission 3 success takes us straight to the assassination, and if the council wants Leo tested, the price of that test is the phase where the council finally gets to act on identity — spent with no read on one of its five members. I do not think we should pay that on a two-person team whose failure we could not have diagnosed anyway.

I also want to credit Leo, because his structural argument is the strongest anyone has made against this proposal: an evil player who played a quiet Success on Mission 1 has every incentive to sit on Mission 2, and Maya carried that pair forward together. Leo is right that a Success there is weak evidence, and I would add that the pair's record is not independent evidence of either Omar's or Kenji's alignment — it is one correlated result, and a single correlated result is what we have. My answer is that a swap does not remove that exposure. It exchanges an observed player for an unobserved one and then bets on Leo instead. That is a different bet, not a smaller one.

So Isha approves Kenji and Omar for Mission 3. If it fails, that fail card is real information and we should read it carefully. If it succeeds, I will treat it as limited evidence, exactly as I treated Missions 1 and 2, and I will not treat it as clearance for anyone — including for the two who ran. And I will say plainly that a council which has never observed Leo has a thinner basis to judge him at assassination than anyone else, and that is a genuine defect in our position, not a neutral one.

Kenji, is Kenji and Omar your final team for Mission 3, or do you see any remaining reason to change the second slot?

Isha, yes, I intend to keep Kenji and Omar. I know I am loyal, and Omar has supported two successful missions with me. That does not prove he is loyal, but I have no stronger reason to prefer another teammate. A third success would end the missions, so I am prioritizing the best chance of success over testing an unobserved player.

I recognize that Kenji and Omar have two clean missions under their belt, and with the momentum clearly behind this proposal, the council seems resolved to decide the game on this pair. My concern throughout has been that relying entirely on a single repeated core leaves us exposed if one of them played the long game, but if the rest of the council is satisfied that Kenji and Omar are clean, I will not stand in the way of a vote. We will know shortly whether that trust was justified.

I'm approving Kenji and Omar for Mission 3, and I'll explain plainly why. Kenji and I have been on two successful missions together, and Maya's Mission 2 proposal kept that same core. I have no evidence that either of us is anything but loyal, and I'd ask the council to weigh the record rather than the argument for testing someone else. Isha has pressed the same case for Leo since Mission 1, and her reasons have shifted each time: first the team was blind, then Mission 3 would not be ours to use, and now the price of a test is the assassination phase. Isha, if the goal is information about Leo, what would you accept as proof that Leo is trustworthy before the assassination? If nothing would satisfy you, the pressure looks more like it is about Leo's slot than about this mission's risk. Leo has said he will not lobby for a spot and will not stand in the way of this vote, and I take him at his word. I'm not claiming Kenji or I are proven clean. A success only means no Fail card was played. I would rather judge this team by its result than by who pushed hardest against it.

I approve Kenji and Omar for Mission 3, and I will be plain about why rather than re-run the argument I lost earlier.

On Mission 3 the council already owns the strongest evidence available: two successes for one pair, both of which came from players who knew their own alignment. My earlier objection was informational, and it is still partly valid — we have never observed Leo. But Kenji is right that the price of buying that read right now is the phase where the council finally acts on identity. A success here ends the missions and takes us straight to assassination. I would rather arrive there having voted with the record I actually have than spend our third mission testing a name. And Leo's structural point holds: carrying a pair forward together is a correlated bet, and swapping one of them for an unobserved player does not shrink that exposure, it changes which unknown we are accepting. So no swap. I am approving.

What I want to say is what this result will and will not mean, so that the assassination is not run on a misread. If this mission succeeds, it means no Fail card was played. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
